claims.claim: Q1 (entity pool ALLOC): arm9 function 0x020834D4 is a generic fixed-capacity pooled-entity constructor, reached from the known MoveInfo-allocator neighborhood via its trampoline 0x02083624 (itself called from the hitbox-processing loop arm9:0x02085704) and, in ov6, from at least two other call sites (0x02164F0C/0x02164F48/0x02168E44). Mechanics: it dereferences a single global singleton pointer (literal value 0x0214BE14) to get a 'manager' object, then reads manager->+0x14 directly as the candidate new-entity pointer (r4); if that is NULL it returns 0 immediately (pool exhausted -- no malloc/new is attempted, consistent with a fixed-size slot pool rather than a general heap alloc). It then invokes a CALLER-SUPPLIED constructor callback via blx on the acquired entity (r4), and stores the callback's return value at entity+0x30 (this is the exact field later read as the 'hitbox/effect record' pointer elsewhere, e.g. arm9:0x02085704's r8=[r6+0x30] and ov6:0x02164EC0/0x02164F80's r7=[r5+0x30]). Depending on whether any init sub-step failed (accumulated in r5), it then calls the generic list-unlink utility 0x2037c24 on &manager+0x14 (removing the entity from whatever list is anchored there) and the generic list-append utility 0x2037b98 on EITHER &manager+0xc (success path) OR &manager+0x1c (failure path) before returning the entity pointer (or 0 on failure). This is a textbook free-list/active-list pooled-object allocator: a global manager with (at least) three list anchors at +0xc, +0x14 and +0x1c, and the same unlink-from-+0x14-then-append-elsewhere pattern on both the success and failure paths.
open_questions: The exact semantic names of manager+0xc/+0x14/+0x1c (my working hypothesis: +0x14=free-list anchor, +0xc=active-list anchor, +0x1c=a 'failed/pending' list) are inferred from control flow, not from any symbol; a live GDB session dumping *0x0214BE14 and walking the three list anchors while spawning/killing a hitbox would confirm which is which.

The runtime address bound to the global variable at literal 0x0214BE14 is outside every query.py-mapped region (arm9 ROM code + ov0-13 ROM code); it resolves at runtime to a RAM location (EWRAM/ITCM), so its live value cannot be inspected statically -- only its 31 literal-load use sites (all in arm9 0x02083xxx-0x02083Bxx) were enumerated.

claims.claim: Q1 (entity pool FREE / despawn primitive): arm9 function 0x02083648 is the destructor counterpart to the 0x020834D4 pooled-entity constructor, and is called from 32 sites across the codebase (2 in arm9's own object module, 30 in ov6). It: (1) sets bit 0 of the entity's own +0x2c flags word ('marked dead'); (2) calls an on-destroy hook via the entity's +0x10 field (the same field 0x020834D4 populates from callee 0x0207c988); (3) unlinks the entity from the manager's +0xc list via the SAME generic list-unlink utility (0x2037c24) that 0x020834D4's success path used to APPEND it there -- i.e. this removes it from the active-entity list; (4) appends the entity to the manager's +0x1c list via 0x2037b98 -- the SAME list-and-utility pair that 0x020834D4's FAILURE path used. This confirms +0xc is the live/active-entity list and +0x1c is a 'retire/pending' list shared by both the failed-construction path and the explicit-destroy path, giving a complete, symmetric alloc/free cycle for the pooled entity type used by projectiles and other spawned hitbox/effect objects.
open_questions: Finalizer 0x2083c44 (checked separately) indexes a per-category table via the entity's +0x38 byte (set to 0xFF/-1 by the constructor at 0x02083520, and set to -1 again by 0x02083648's own finalizer path) to do further per-category-list bookkeeping; its exact role (recycling the slot back to the +0x14 free list vs. deferred cleanup) was not traced this round.

claims.claim: Q2 (spawn path, mechanics of the dispatcher): ov6 function 0x021574CC is a 13-way (index 0..0xc) switch/event dispatcher keyed on its 3rd argument (r2), operating directly on the CHARACTER struct (r1 -> r4, using the ground-truth-confirmed fields +0x1a4 hit-tally and +0x1a8 MoveInfo). Case index 8 (jump-table target 0x2157684) unconditionally reaches, via straight-line code with no intervening conditional branch, a call to ov6:0x2168cf4 at 0x02157700, passing r1 = [r4, #0x1a8] (the character's MoveInfo pointer, loaded immediately before the call) and r0 = a per-move 'collision-entry-set' base pointer (ip, itself obtained a few instructions earlier from [[r4,#0x1a0]+r6*4]+0x18c). Two signed bytes at offsets +0x1a and +0x1b of a nested sub-object (r8 = that collision-entry-set's own +8 field) are read and packed into the stack-passed argument block right before the call, and a value looked up from a small jump table indexed by a byte at [ip,#0x8c] is also packed in -- i.e. per-move collision/type data is what parameterizes the entity that gets created.
open_questions: Which caller invokes 0x021574CC with the selector r2=8 (this dispatcher itself has 0 static callers found by query.py, i.e. it is only reached indirectly, presumably via a vtable/function-pointer slot on the character struct) was not traced this round -- it is the missing link back to 'an attack with projectileId!=0 fires'. A companion case (index 9, target 0x21575e8) independently reads the SAME sub-object's +0x1b byte and compares it to 2 (not 1) as part of its own validation, which is suggestive that +0x1b is a small move-kind/type enum, but this was not proven to be literally the on-disk CollisionEntry.ProjectileId byte (src/JUS.Tool/Combat/Formats/CollisionEntry.cs, offset +3 in the 20-byte on-disk record) or CollisionType (offset +0, where collisionType=4 is the ground-truth projectile-hitbox category) -- that provenance chain (disk record -> loaded runtime sub-object +0x1b) is unresolved.

GDB check to settle the open question above: break at ov6:0x021576C0, dump the byte at [r8+0x1b] and the current move's on-disk CollisionEntry.ProjectileId/CollisionType for a character with a known projectile move (bb_b_01 or db_b_01 per collision-data.round1.json, whose only two nonzero-projectileId=-32 entries both have collisionType=4), and confirm whether they correlate.

claims.claim: Q2/Q4 (spawn + ownership): ov6 function 0x02168CF4 (called from the case-8 dispatch above) captures its 2nd argument as r4 (= the MoveInfo pointer passed in) for its entire body -- it is never reassigned. After several position/bounds computations, it obtains a small 'spawner/wrapper' object r6 from an ov6-local manager rooted at a second global (literal 0x02172990, distinct from the arm9 pool manager at 0x0214BE14), then at 0x02168E44 calls bl 0x020834D4 (the pooled-entity constructor confirmed in the Q1 claims above) with flags built from #0x800 and a couple of bic-masked immediates, storing the newly pool-allocated entity pointer into wrapper+8 (0x02168E48: str r0,[r6,#8]). Immediately after, at 0x02168E5C, it stores r4 -- the MoveInfo pointer received as this function's own argument -- into wrapper+0xc (str r4,[r6,#0xc]). This is a concrete ownership back-pointer: the freshly spawned pooled entity's wrapper object records, at a fixed offset (+0xc), a pointer back to the attacking character's MoveInfo object (itself a per-character field at character+0x1a8 per prior-round ground truth), i.e. one indirection removed from the character struct itself rather than a direct character-struct pointer.
open_questions: Whether wrapper+0xc (MoveInfo pointer) is the ONLY ownership reference, or whether the pooled entity itself (at wrapper+8, i.e. the object 0x020834D4 actually constructs) also stores a more direct character-struct back-pointer at some offset inside its own layout -- this was not checked this round; the constructor callback used for THIS spawn path (the ctor fn pointer argument to 0x020834D4 at 0x02168E44, loaded from a stack slot rather than a fixed literal, so it was not statically resolved) would need to be identified to answer that.

If wrapper+0xc is the sole ownership link, a character-switch teardown that frees/nulls the MoveInfo object at character+0x1a8 would orphan the pointer (dangling, not crashing, since the entity doesn't necessarily dereference it every frame) rather than cause an immediate teardown of the spawned entity -- this is circumstantial support for the Q5 persistence hypothesis but was not directly observed (see the dedicated Q5 open question in suggested_next_angles).

claims.claim: Q3 (despawn / per-frame kill conditions): ov6 function 0x0216C958 (size 404 bytes) contains a per-entity per-frame check block (0x0216CA00-0x0216CAE8) with FOUR independent conditions that each converge on calling the destroy primitive arm9:0x02083648 (confirmed in the Q1-free claim above) and then returning 0: (a) a flag-bit gate -- [some_field+0x78]&0xf, plus [entity+8]->+8 bit 0x1000, plus [some_field+0x38] bit 0x1, plus the return value of a helper at 0x216ee14 (shape consistent with an off-screen/wall/collision boundary test) -- any of the latter three being true leads straight to destroy at 0x0216CA44; (b) an explicit 16-bit AGE COUNTER at entity+4 that is incremented every call (ldrsh, +1, strh back) and compared against a hard threshold of 0x20 (32) -- once the pre-increment value exceeds 32, it falls through to a second destroy call at 0x0216CA8C (classic frame-count lifetime-expiry timer); (c) a 32-bit field read via a separate pointer (r4, not saved/traced further this round) compared against 0x100, gating a third destroy call at 0x0216CAB4; (d) the same r4 field compared against a second (larger) literal threshold, gating a fourth destroy call at 0x0216CAE0, with the 'still alive' path returning 1 only when under BOTH thresholds. Every one of the four kill sites clears a bit in a local flags byte at [entity_ptr,#6] before calling destroy.
open_questions: The exact object identity of r4 (used for the +0x100 / second-threshold checks) and the semantic meaning of helper 0x216ee14 (my structural read: an off-screen/wall/collision boundary test, by analogy with similar per-frame update loops in this overlay, but its own body was not disassembled this round) were not traced -- a live GDB session breaking at 0x0216CA28 and 0x0216CA98 while a projectile move plays out (e.g. a known ranged character) would settle both the off-screen-check hypothesis and the r4 field's meaning (candidate: total distance travelled or a hit counter).

Whether this exact 0x0216C958 update function specifically handles PROJECTILE-class entities (vs. some other spawned hitbox/effect type sharing the same 0x02083648 destroy primitive) was not confirmed by tracing a call chain back from the case-8/0x2168cf4 spawn path of the Q2 claims to this specific update function; they are linked only by both using the same generic pool alloc/free (0x020834D4/0x02083648), not by a directly observed caller-callee edge this round.

suggested_next_angles: Q5 (persistence across character switch) was NOT resolved this round and no claim was made about it, per the no-guessing rule. What WAS established: the pooled entity's only observed ownership back-pointer (wrapper+0xc, Q4 claim) points at the attacking character's MoveInfo object, not at the character struct directly, and the entity's despawn conditions (Q3 claim) are purely self-contained (age counter, boundary/collision helper, two threshold checks on an internal field) with no observed check of 'is my owning character still the active/on-screen one'. Neither fact directly proves persistence, but both are consistent with it. The missing piece is the character-switch/tag-out teardown function itself: search for a function that reads character+0x1a8 (MoveInfo) and either frees it or nulls it (candidate signature: takes the character struct, at some point does 'ldr r0,[rX,#0x1a8]; cmp r0,#0; bl <free-like-callee>'), then check whether THAT function also walks the arm9 manager's active list (&*0x0214BE14+0xc) or the ov6-local manager rooted at literal 0x02172990 -- if it does neither, that is direct confirming evidence that projectile/effect entities are NOT torn down by character switch.

The ov6-local secondary manager rooted at literal 0x02172990 (referenced from ov6:0x02168DBC/0x02168F10/0x02168F24/0x02169000/0x02169014/0x021691E4/0x021694AC/0x02169518, i.e. a cluster spanning 0x02168xxx-0x02169xxx) appears to be a second, more specific active-object list layered on top of the generic arm9 pool manager (0x0214BE14) -- e.g. 'active projectiles/effects in this battle' vs. 'all pooled game objects globally'. Its exact relationship to the arm9 manager (does it hold the SAME entity pointers, or wrapper objects one level up as seen at wrapper+8?) was only partially traced (Q2/Q4 claims) and deserves a dedicated round if per-projectile bookkeeping (e.g. a projectile counter/cap per character) is the next research target.

The finalizer functions 0x2083cd8 and 0x2083c44 (both called from inside the alloc/free pair, keyed off the entity's +0x38 category byte and a per-category 8-byte table at [*0x0214BE14 + 0x74 + category*8]) look like a category-indexed secondary bookkeeping layer (possibly per-hitbox-type free-lists, e.g. separating projectiles from generic hit-effects from smoke/dust particles) that would be worth resolving if the goal becomes distinguishing 'projectile entity' from 'generic spawned hitbox/effect entity' at the type-tag level, since Q1-Q4 this round establish the SHARED pool mechanism but do not prove projectiles get a distinct category value from other spawned objects.
